nameStory: Lady's bedstraw earned its charming name from medieval times when people stuffed mattresses with its dried stems and leaves. The plant's sweet, honey-like fragrance made bedrooms smell pleasant, and it was believed to repel fleas and other pests. Legend even says that Mary used lady's bedstraw as bedding in the manger where Jesus was born, which is why it's sometimes called "Our Lady's bedstraw."
description: Lady's bedstraw is a cheerful perennial wildflower that creates clouds of tiny yellow blooms in summer. This upright plant grows 2-4 feet tall with stiff, square stems that feel sturdy to the touch. Its narrow, dark green leaves grow in neat circles around the stem, creating a distinctive whorled pattern that makes it easy to spot even before it flowers. When in full bloom, the dense clusters of bright yellow flowers create a frothy, almost foam-like appearance.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny bright yellow flowers, each only about 1/8 inch across, clustered together in dense, frothy masses at the top of stems. The flowers have four petals and emit a sweet, honey-like fragrance that's especially noticeable on warm days.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, linear leaves about 1 inch long arranged in whorls of 8-12 around the stem, creating a distinctive spoke-like pattern. Leaves feel slightly rough and are shiny dark green on top, with tiny hairs underneath that you can feel when you rub them.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright, bushy plant 2-4 feet tall with multiple stiff, four-angled stems that feel square when rolled between your fingers. Forms colonies that spread by underground rhizomes.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Square stems that feel rigid and sturdy, not hollow like grass stems. The four-sided shape is easily felt when you gently squeeze or roll the stem between your thumb and finger.

habitat: Lady's bedstraw thrives in sunny, open areas with well-drained soils, especially in fields, meadows, roadsides, and disturbed ground. You'll often find it in sandy or rocky soils where other plants struggle, and it's commonly seen along railroad tracks and in old pastures. It prefers full sun and can tolerate dry conditions once established.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as clusters of narrow leaves in distinctive whorled arrangements around square stems. Plants are low and bushy but haven't yet developed their full height.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time from June through August, when plants are covered in masses of tiny, fragrant yellow flowers. This is when the plant is most noticeable and easiest to identify from a distance.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and stems begin to brown, but the distinctive leaf arrangement and square stems remain visible. Seeds develop but are tiny and inconspicuous.
seasonality.winter: Dried brown stems may persist above ground, showing the characteristic branching pattern, though most of the plant dies back to underground parts.

funFact: Lady's bedstraw contains natural compounds that can actually curdle milk, making it a traditional cheese-making ingredient! In some parts of Europe, it's still used to make a special yellow cheese, and the plant was so valuable for this purpose that it was once traded like a spice.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other white-flowered bedstraws like hedge bedstraw, but lady's bedstraw is the only common bedstraw with bright yellow flowers in New England. The yellow blooms make it quite distinctive among its relatives, which typically have white or greenish flowers.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name, lady's bedstraw is not native to North America but was brought by European settlers who valued it for practical uses like mattress stuffing, cheese-making, and dyeing cloth yellow. It has naturalized widely and is now considered part of New England's naturalized flora.
compareHints: Lady's bedstraw stands out among New England's bedstraws because of its bright yellow flowers - most other bedstraw species have white or greenish blooms. It's also more upright and robust than sprawling species like catchweed bedstraw, and lacks the sweet vanilla scent of sweet woodruff when crushed. The combination of yellow flowers, whorled leaves, and square stems makes it unmistakable among its relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's bedstraws, catchweed is unique for its extremely clingy nature and annual growth habit.

Hedge bedstraw differs from other common bedstraws by its smooth stems and purely white flowers - catchweed bedstraw has sticky stems, lady's bedstraw has yellow flowers, and fragrant bedstraw has a sweet vanilla scent when crushed.
Unlike its weedy cousin catchweed bedstraw which grabs onto your clothes with hooked bristles, sweet woodruff stays put and feels soft to touch.
Among New England's bedstraws, fragrant bedstraw is unique for its sweet vanilla scent when crushed – most other bedstraws are odorless or have different scents.
Among New England's 15+ bedstraw species, licorice bedstraw stands out with its consistently four broad, oval leaves per whorl - most others have 6-8 narrow, linear leaves arranged in circles.
Marsh-bedstraw is distinguished from other bedstraws by its preference for consistently wet habitats and its delicate, mat-forming growth pattern.
Among New England's bedstraws, rough bedstraw is distinguished by its prominent stem hooks and preference for wet areas.
Unlike catchweed bedstraw with its velcro-like sticky stems or sweet woodruff's hay-like fragrance, Torrey's wild licorice has smooth stems and that distinctive taste.
Unlike catchweed bedstraw which has sticky, grabby stems and four-petaled flowers, three-petal bedstraw feels smoother and has its distinctive three-petaled blooms.
Among the 15+ bedstraw species in New England, stiff marsh bedstraw is one of only two with 3-petaled flowers (the other being three-petal bedstraw).
Among New England's bedstraws, hairy bedstraw is unique for its consistently soft, fuzzy texture throughout the plant.

White bedstraw differs from other New England bedstraws by its upright growth habit and smooth stems - catchweed bedstraw has hooked bristles that grab onto clothing, while lady's bedstraw has bright yellow flowers instead of white.
Unlike the common catchweed bedstraw with its grabby, rough stems, boreal bedstraw is soft and non-sticky.
Northern bedstraw differs from other New England bedstraws by its upright growth habit and narrow leaves with three parallel veins.
Among New England's bedstraws, bluntleaf bedstraw stands out for its preference for wet habitats and those distinctive rounded leaf tips.
